title: meridian-station-operations-handbook
summary: Operations handbook for Meridian Station, a fictional low-orbit research outpost for materials science, human health, and cargo craft staging. Covers the four-module layout with a table of module purposes and crew capacities, the four-person crew roster with roles and shifts (day 06:00–14:00, night 14:00–22:00, shared quiet hours 22:00–06:00), and life-support systems including oxygen reserves by module (Figure 1 bar chart: Habitat 1 92%, Habitat 2 81%, Laboratory 67%, Cargo 54%), water recovery (~93%), and cabin targets (21 °C, 101 kPa). Also gives required responses for fire, hull breach, and evacuation, including who decides evacuation, where the repair kit is kept, and escape capsule capacity (four seats, three days of supplies).

children.title: Overview
children.summary: Introduces Meridian Station, a fictional low-orbit research outpost focused on materials science, human health, and staging cargo craft visits, and states the handbook's purpose of describing day-to-day operations. It also describes the station layout: four pressurized modules (Habitat 1, Habitat 2, Laboratory, Cargo) joined by a central node, each with an independent life-support loop so problems can be isolated. A table lists each module's purpose and crew capacity, useful for questions about module functions or how many crew each can hold.
children.text:
Mission
Meridian Station is a fictional low-orbit research outpost. Its mission is to run long-duration experiments in materials science and human health, and to serve as a staging point for short visits by cargo craft. This handbook describes how the station is run day to day.

Station layout
The station has four pressurized modules connected by a central node. Each module has its own life-support loop, so a problem in one module can be sealed off from the others.

| Module | Purpose | Crew capacity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Habitat 1 | Sleeping quarters and galley | 4 |
| Habitat 2 | Exercise and medical bay | 2 |
| Laboratory | Experiments and workstations | 3 |
| Cargo | Supplies and spare parts | 1 |

children.title: Crew and Roles
children.summary: Lists the current four-person crew, who rotates every six months, with each member's role and shift (Ada Okonkwo, Commander, Day; Luis Vargas, Flight Engineer, Night; Priya Nair, Medical Officer, Day; Tomasz Wrona, Systems Specialist, Night). Also covers shift hours: day shift 06:00–14:00 and night shift 14:00–22:00 station time, with 22:00–06:00 as a shared rest period during which only the duty alarm may wake the crew. Useful for questions about who holds which role, shift timings, or quiet hours. Contains one roster table.
children.text:
Roster
The current four-person crew rotates every six months.

| Name | Role | Shift |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ada Okonkwo | Commander | Day |
| Luis Vargas | Flight Engineer | Night |
| Priya Nair | Medical Officer | Day |
| Tomasz Wrona | Systems Specialist | Night |

Shift schedule
Day shift runs 06:00 to 14:00 station time and night shift runs 14:00 to 22:00. The hours from 22:00 to 06:00 are a shared rest period, and only the duty alarm may wake the crew.

children.title: Life Support
children.summary: Covers how the station supplies and regulates its life-support systems: oxygen production from recycled water with shift-by-shift reserve checks and a 50 percent commander-notification floor, water recovery at about 93 percent with the remainder resupplied by cargo craft, and cabin temperature (21 °C) and pressure (101 kPa) targets with a pressure-drop alarm. Figure 1, a bar chart, compares oxygen reserves by module: Habitat 1 at 92%, Habitat 2 at 81%, Laboratory at 67%, and Cargo at 54%.
children.text:
Oxygen supply
Oxygen is produced by electrolysis of recycled water and stored in tanks in each module. Reserves are checked every shift. A module must never drop below 50 percent of tank capacity without the commander being told.

[image:img-1]

Figure 1. Oxygen reserve by module, as a percent of capacity: Habitat 1 at 92, Habitat 2 at 81, Laboratory at 67, Cargo at 54.

Water recycling
About 93 percent of water, including humidity from the air and treated wastewater, is recovered and reused. The remaining loss is made up from tanks delivered by cargo craft.

Temperature and pressure
Cabin temperature is held at 21 degrees Celsius and pressure at 101 kilopascals. An alarm sounds if pressure falls by more than 3 kilopascals within ten minutes.

children.title: Emergency Procedures
children.summary: Covers the crew's required responses to three emergencies: fire (sound the alarm, shut module ventilation, use the nearest extinguisher, never open a burning module's hatch, report to the commander at the central node), hull breach (seal the affected module on a pressure alarm, count crew at the central node, Systems Specialist locates and patches the leak using the repair kit in the Cargo module), and evacuation (crew boards the escape capsule at the central node when the station cannot be made safe; the commander decides; the capsule seats four and carries three days of supplies). Useful for questions about who decides evacuation, where the repair kit is stored, or capsule capacity. No tables or images.
children.text:
Fire
Sound the alarm, shut the module's ventilation, and use the nearest extinguisher. Never open a hatch to a module that is on fire. Report to the commander from the central node.

Hull breach
When the pressure alarm sounds, move to the nearest hatch and seal the affected module. Count the crew at the central node. The Systems Specialist then locates the leak using the pressure map and patches it with the repair kit stored in the Cargo module.

Evacuation
If the station cannot be made safe, the crew boards the escape capsule docked at the central node. The commander decides when to evacuate. The capsule seats four and carries three days of supplies.
